mainEntity.name: Are my teeth actually crooked if they look uneven in selfies?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Smartphone cameras use wide-angle lenses that distort facial proportions, often making central features appear larger and peripheral features smaller. This can create the impression that your teeth are more uneven than they actually are. The only reliable way to determine whether your teeth are genuinely misaligned is through a clinical dental examination, which includes a thorough assessment of your bite, tooth positioning, and overall oral health. If selfies are your primary source of concern, try photographing your smile from a greater distance to reduce lens distortion.

mainEntity.name: Why do I look different in photos compared to the mirror?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mirrors show a laterally reversed image of your face — the version you see every day and are most familiar with. Photographs show your face as others see it, which is non-reversed. Because your brain is accustomed to your mirrored image, the photographic version can look subtly unfamiliar, and minor asymmetries that your brain normally filters out may become more noticeable. This is a well-documented psychological phenomenon known as the mere-exposure effect and applies to all facial features, not just your teeth.

mainEntity.name: Can uneven teeth be a sign of a dental problem?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases, teeth that appear or feel uneven may indicate an underlying dental concern. Tooth crowding, bite irregularities, gum recession, or progressive tooth wear can all contribute to visible asymmetry. If you have noticed a change in your tooth alignment over time, or if you experience symptoms such as difficulty chewing, jaw discomfort, or sensitivity, it would be sensible to arrange a dental assessment. Your dentist can evaluate whether any clinical intervention might be appropriate based on your individual circumstances.

mainEntity.name: Do teeth become more uneven with age?

acceptedAnswer.text: Teeth can shift gradually throughout life due to natural changes in bone density, gum tissue, and the forces applied during chewing. A phenomenon known as mesial drift causes teeth to move slowly forward over time. Additionally, tooth wear, gum recession, and loss of bone support can contribute to changes in alignment. Wearing retainers after orthodontic treatment, maintaining excellent oral hygiene, and attending regular dental reviews can help minimise age-related changes to your tooth positioning.

mainEntity.name: Should I consider treatment if I am unhappy with how my teeth look in photos?

acceptedAnswer.text: If your concern is primarily related to photographic distortion, it is worth experimenting with different camera settings, angles, and lighting before considering dental treatment. However, if you are consistently unhappy with the appearance of your teeth in both photographs and day-to-day life, a dental consultation may help clarify whether there is an underlying alignment, wear, or gum-related issue worth addressing. Treatment is not always necessary, and where it is considered, suitability will depend on a thorough clinical examination and your individual circumstances.

mainEntity.name: Can a dentist tell whether the issue is real or just camera distortion?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A dentist can assess whether the appearance of uneven teeth is most likely due to photographic distortion, normal anatomical variation, or a genuine dental concern such as crowding, tooth wear, bite imbalance, or gum recession. Clinical examination, photographs, and where appropriate dental imaging can provide a much more reliable picture than selfies alone. This can be reassuring if the issue is mostly optical, and helpful if any underlying dental changes do need monitoring.
